title: bim-bench: AIは BIM モデルの空間構造をどこまで読めるか
description:
A benchmark measuring how far large language models can read the spatial structure of a building from IFC: the site-building-storey-space hierarchy, which elements belong to which storey, and the quantities attached to them.

IFC is a graph, not a drawing, so the questions have exact answers that a parser can confirm. The corpus is buildingSMART's own Sample-Test-Files, published under CC BY 4.0 and bundled here with attribution.

Principal finding: accuracy and cost separate in opposite directions. Arm B (no code execution) reached 235/255 on element attribution at 372k tokens and 36 minutes; arm C (Python permitted) reached 255/255 at 99k tokens and 9 minutes — better on every axis at roughly a quarter of the cost. Arm C additionally declined to trust a quantity field it could not verify, and derived the volumes independently.

IFC に入っている空間構造・要素の所属・数量を読み取る能力を測る。コード実行を許した腕が、点数でもコストでも上回った。

Part of the AI Practical Reach Index, a series applying one common yardstick across Japanese professional domains.

Version 1.2.0 reports that repairing the v1.1.0 defect introduced a worse one. The note written to document it printed the answers to four of the repaired task's thirteen questions — the four the repair existed to ask. All three solver runs reported it independently; five checks passed the statement carrying them, including a scope check written for the previous defect. The task is recorded as a failed measurement and left unrepaired.

A second re-issue with the numbers removed succeeded: both arms reached 13/13, no run reported a disclosure, and the diagnosis behind the repair is supported. During that run the operator became an examination-side defect, misreading a slow delegate transport as a broken one and instructing two running solvers to truncate. The one that complied returned 7/13, wrong by exactly one on all six counting questions; the one that refused returned 13/13 and reported the misdiagnosis. The freeze held throughout and did not help — it constrains artefacts and says nothing about the operator's conduct during a run.

A claim that this task's cost comparison was void is withdrawn: re-running the read-only arm with its faulty tool description corrected cost three per cent more, inside its own run-to-run spread. Also added: checks for answer disclosure and for questions reachable by a shallower route than intended, a two-tier hash freeze covering the prompt the solver actually reads, and the finding that a few dozen corpus lines individually exceed the read tool's cap and are therefore unreadable by the no-execution arm.

Version 1.2.1 adds the post-hoc baseline records that were missing from T001 through T005. The accompanying paper stated that already-run tasks carried a baseline hash record; in this repository five of them did not, and the freeze verifier passed anyway, because a missing record is not drift. The baseline mode itself had never been implemented here — only the pre-run freeze, which refuses to stamp once answers exist — so there was no command that could record these tasks at all. A baseline does not certify the past; it only makes later drift detectable, and the records name what could not be captured: the solver prompts for these five tasks were never retained.
